the following factors are important to understanding the current state of local renewable energy policy and program development in both New York and London: (1) the presence or lack thereof of formal regulatory mechanisms; (2) the existence or lack of an urban growth coalition; and (3) the existence or absence of a local environmental coalition.

the question of why, despite growing attention to the importance of urban sustainability and steady increases in overall use of different renewables power technologies around the country, New York City and other cities tend to have low levels of green power use or renewables deployment within their borders.
how the institutional context of local energy policy-making and the nature of the regime that is formed to implement it influence local renewable energy program outcomes.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the most significant factor in explaining the lack of renewable energy use in cities is the highly regulated nature of the electric power sector, which constrains the ability of local actors to implement policies or programs that might otherwise have been successful.

urban policy-makers in both New York and London are constrained by the regulatory environment of the electric power sector, which in turn is heavily influenced by the national government's energy policies.
urban regimes are not the only actors that shape urban energy policy, and that the influence of formal regulations and other institutional factors should not be ignored.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the most important factors that influence urban energy policy are the formal, regulatory environment, as well as the informal, institutionalized relationships between the various actors that are involved in the policy process.
the electric power industry's policy environment is highly constraining on local governments and their efforts to implement renewable energy projects.

the institutional environment in which energy policy-making takes place has a strong influence on the decisions that are ultimately made, and that urban regime analysis, when combined with new institutionalist approaches, is an effective way to understand the factors that lead to these decisions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the policy and regulatory environment surrounding energy policy-making in the United States is highly constraining.
urban energy policy-making and program implementation can be best understood through a hybrid approach that combines the insights of new institutionalism and urban governance theories.
the policy environment for energy policy-making is much more complex than is generally understood.
